query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The high configurational entropy inherent in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) lowers the effective activation energies for selective outward diffusion of oxide‐forming elements (e.g., Al and Cr), enabling rapid nucleation and stabilization of a coherent, defect‐controlled protective oxide layer that remains adherent under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, multi-principal-element HEA without a preformed oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA to high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 800–1100 °C in controlled oxygen partial pressure) while comparing with a conventional alloy having similar overall chemistry but lower configurational entropy.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidizing environment with controlled temperature, oxygen partial pressure, and exposure duration typical for high-temperature applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Selective elemental diffusion pathways and the resulting localized segregation at the alloy surface that promotes the formation of dense, coherent Al2O3 or Cr2O3 phase(s).
generation.mechanism: DFT and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations predict that the high configurational entropy in HEAs leads to a broadened distribution of diffusion activation energies, which facilitates the selective and faster outward migration of protective oxide-forming elements. This promotes the nucleation of a dense, defect-controlled oxide scale that resists spallation and excessive growth by limiting further oxygen ingress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline conventional alloy, the HEA will form a thinner, more uniform, and adherent oxide layer with fewer defects, observable as a lower porosity and more consistent elemental distribution in cross-sectional analyses.
generation.baseline: A conventional alloy of similar composition but with lower or negligible configurational entropy, where oxide layers develop in a less controlled manner, possibly with higher porosity or non-uniform elemental distribution.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies under high-temperature conditions (800–1100 °C) in oxidizing environments; deviations in temperature, extreme oxygen partial pressures, or different oxide-forming element concentrations can alter the diffusion and oxidation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative impact of configurational entropy on the diffusion activation energies and defect formation energies is uncertain, and precise energy barriers vary with specific alloy compositions. Further experimental validation is needed to isolate the entropy effect from other contributing factors.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of HEAs with high configurational entropy and a comparable set of conventional alloys with similar overall composition but ordered structures. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions (800–1100 °C, controlled oxygen atmosphere). Conduct cross-sectional microscopy (e.g., SEM) and compositional mapping (e.g., EDS) to evaluate oxide layer thickness, uniformity, and defect density. Additionally, measure diffusion activation energies using tracer diffusion experiments or in situ high-temperature analyses.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity via cross-sectional imaging.
Elemental distributions at the oxide–metal interface.
Diffusion activation energies and defect concentrations derived from experimental or simulated analyses.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not show significantly lower effective diffusion activation energies, nor the formation of a denser (more uniform and adherent) protective oxide layer compared to the conventional alloy under the same conditions, then the hypothesis that configurational entropy drives enhanced protective oxide formation is falsified.

In this study, CrMnFeCoNi HEA behaviour responding to changes in temperature and environmental factors such as the partial pressure of oxygen has been investigated by in situ XRD at high temperatures up to 1100 °C. In situ thermal observations of materials with the high-temperature XRD provide unique information such as temperature-dependent phase transformations, types of new phase formation, and the start and finish temperatures of competing phases in an alloy system []. In situ HTXRD is instrumental in revealing the real-time of oxide formation as well as the type and temperature at which various kinds of oxide form when metals are exposed to high temperatures in air or in another simulated environment. Our HTXRD analysis provided insight into the thermal stability, phase transitions, and high-temperature oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy samples, which provides significant guidance in the development of high-performance alloys for demanding applications. The surface and cross-sectional microstructure, elemental distributions, and oxide compositions have been examined to further understand the evolution of the oxides. Diffusion in materials dictates the kinetics of precipitation, new phase formation and microstructure evolution, and strongly influences mechanical and physical properties. For example, altering nanoprecipitate size and dispersion by thermal processing enables substantial increases in strength and good ductility in multicomponent alloys,. Essentially rooted in diffusion kinetics, predicting how fast local composition and microstructure evolve is a fundamental goal of material science. In metals and alloys, diffusion processes are connected with vacancies, point defects that mediate atom jumps in the crystal lattice. Molecular dynamics (MD) modeling based on force fields or density functional theory, which probe the atomic mechanisms of diffusion at a nanosecond timescale, are often not able to access slow diffusion kinetics-induced microstructure change. To circumvent this time limitation inherent in MD, the kinetic Monte Carlo method (kMC) is primarily adopted to model diffusion-mediated structure evolution, for instance, the early stage of precipitation in dilute alloys,. frame.system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) designed for high‐temperature oxidation, initially as a homogenized, multi-principal-element alloy without a preformed oxide layer.
frame.goal: To mechanistically understand how these alloys develop and maintain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance, by identifying the atomic-scale processes that govern oxide nucleation, growth, and stability.
frame.limitation: Current studies do not clearly distinguish how the complex elemental interactions and resulting microsegregations in HEAs uniquely promote the formation of a coherent, defect-controlled oxide compared to conventional alloys.
root_cause_cues: ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer
what governs the behaviour and why
observations expected relative to a baseline
result that would falsify the hypothesis
constraints: Must propose a single, testable mechanistic hypothesis
Needs to specify the governing factors (e.g., specific elemental contributions, defect chemistry, diffusion kinetics)
Requires a controlled experimental design for direct comparison with a traditional alloy baseline
The hypothesis must define the operative boundaries and provide clear criteria for falsification
frame.regime: High-temperature, oxidizing conditions that simulate service environments (e.g., controlled oxygen partial pressures, specific temperature ranges, and exposure durations typical for high-temperature applications).
prior_attempts: Prior work on conventional alloys linked oxidation resistance to the presence of reactive elements (such as Cr or Al) but did not isolate the enhanced role of configurational entropy in HEAs.
Earlier studies did not effectively separate the effects of complex diffusion pathways and localized element segregation on protective oxide formation in multi-component systems.

families.principle: Employing computational models (e.g., density functional theory, kinetic Monte Carlo, phase-field simulations) to calculate diffusion kinetics, defect energetics, and segregation phenomena that govern oxide nucleation and the stabilization of a protective scale.
cues_for: role of configurational entropy in defect-controlled oxide growth
cues_against: the requirement for a controlled experimental comparison
simulated conditions may need validation against experimental baselines
families.best_lever: Deploy DFT calculations combined with kinetic Monte Carlo simulations to quantify diffusion activation energies and defect formation energies, thereby linking elemental segregation trends to the onset and stability of the protective oxide.

families.principle: Integrating targeted in situ experiments with atomistic or mesoscale simulations to cross-validate observations and model predictions, thus furnishing a comprehensive mechanistic picture of oxide nucleation and growth influenced by HEA complexity.

cues_against: the increased complexity and resource intensity of combining multiple approaches

families.best_lever: Integrate in situ high-temperature characterization (e.g., ETEM or synchrotron X-ray analysis) with DFT-informed kinetic Monte Carlo simulations to directly correlate observed oxide formation kinetics and microsegregation patterns with simulation-predicted diffusion and defect processes.

families.principle: Real-time, high-resolution observation of oxidation processes at relevant temperatures to capture nucleation, defect creation, and growth kinetics of the protective oxide layer, revealing mechanisms at the atomic or mesoscopic level.

cues_against: the need for a controlled comparison that may be more accessible to conventional experiments

families.best_lever: Utilize in situ environmental transmission electron microscopy (ETEM) or synchrotron based X-ray techniques to dynamically monitor oxide layer nucleation and defect formation under service-like high-temperature conditions.

families.principle: Systematically varying alloy compositions and oxidation conditions to measure differences in oxide layer formation kinetics and defect chemistry, thereby isolating the effect of configurational entropy and elemental contributions.

directly reveal differences between HEAs and traditional alloys
cues_against: defect-controlled oxide formation may be challenging to capture with bulk measurements
families.best_lever: Design an experiment comparing HEAs with a conventional alloy baseline under identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions using detailed oxide scale thickness measurements (e.g., via XRD or SEM) to directly link compositional variations to oxidation kinetics.
